articles.title: A question of region
articles.content: “Don’t know much about history, don’t know much biology,Don’t know much about the science book, don’t know much about the French I took…” THIS is an old song, which seems to be an apt description of journalists — especially in Pakistan. Over the decades, the profession has moved on from print to television and now digital but our training remains rooted in old-fashioned ‘generalism’ (if there’s such a word). As with the bureaucrats who run petroleum one day and health the other, we journalists move from commenting on foreign affairs one evening to the economy and healthcare the next. The notion of specialising in issues or studying them in depth is as alien to us as democracy is to Islamabad’s neighbours. Perhaps this is why most in the profession rarely bother with reading and books. Take history — even of Pakistan. Those of us who entered the field at the time of newspapers learnt the country’s history through oral tradition. Late-night chats with senior colleagues, who had survived martial laws and newsroom working hours, told us of tumultuous times such as war, secession and dictatorship. They included those who remembered what it was like working during the censorship of Ziaul Haq’s times, the night Pervez Musharraf removed the government or when an operation was first launched against the MQM in Karachi. The oral history we learnt alongside copy editing was the best counter-narrative to the whitewashed account taught in school books under Pakistan Studies. Our daastango provided us with a fun but patchy account of the land of the pure. Patchy, for it leaves us with more questions than answers — the personal accounts that we learn history from are rooted in Pakistan but are a little sketchy on details of the region. Few journalists have travelled around the region and reported on other countries. As a result, many may point out similarities between Pakistan and Egypt (aren’t they obvious?) but few will note what makes them different and why. For a hack such as myself, the biggest difference is perhaps Pakistan’s impatience with its rulers. Our last dictator spent eight years in power, struggling in the last two. And in Egypt, Anwar Sadat spent 11 years in power, Hosni Mubarak around three decades, while Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has been ruling for 12 and is still going strong. Closer to Pakistan, the Gulf states in general have also enjoyed stability and long reigns without much pressure from below. Evidently, this is due to oil, but can it explain everything? After all, Iran is no less oil-rich and yet it went through a revolution, which perhaps remains unprecedented as a political event in the region. Despite the authoritarianism of both the Shah and the theocracy that followed, Iran has demonstrated that its people believe in resistance. In recent years, they have pushed back multiple times against crackdowns; at times they have even compelled the state to change course. This is a strain missing in Iran’s neighbours to the west. Crowded, noisy and poor, societies in this region struggle with imperfect democracies. But to its east, it’s a different story. Pakistan and the rest of South Asia, in comparison to its western neighbours in the Middle East, are poorer and noisier. Is this why this region has avoided the kind of authoritarianism that marks the Middle East? Crowded, noisy and poor, societies in this region continue to struggle with flawed and imperfect democracies; there is flirtation with authoritarianism but on paper most of them adhere or aspire to the framework left by the British. This is true of Pakistan where martial law dictators have also worked hard to prove their democratic credentials by holding elections. And with it comes the inability of rulers in the region to lord it over their citizens for long periods. Indeed, in recent years, Hasina Wajed’s 15 years in power has been quite a feat. In India, Jawaharlal Nehru and Narendra Modi have also enjoyed prime ministerships for a similar period of time. On the other hand, in Pakistan, the longest power stints have been a bit shorter. In a tradition closer to Iran, South Asia has also pushed back against dictators of the civilian (Wajed) and military (Musharraf) type, with street protests forcing them to call it a day. Strongmen such as Modi have also been bested by students armed with their wit and social media, while in Pakistan, authoritarian establishments have struggled to clamp down on criticism on X. This is not entirely new: back in the 1970s, both Indira Gandhi’s imposition of the Emergency and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto’s authoritarian rule came to an end, albeit in very different ways. In one country, the democratic system pushed back while in the other, the military establishment did so. With all our problems, Pakistan’s journalists still sit in talk shows and complain about the censorship they face; their counterparts in nearby regions are perhaps not allowed to whine thus on live television. In most countries with censorship, journalists usually spend their time complaining about absolute freedom. There is an ‘argumentative’ South Asian that shapes this region differently from its western neighbours. And perhaps also its eastern ones. Travel east to Myanmar and here once again, regimes tend to become more authoritarian and more long-lasting. The long detention of Aung San Suu Kyi under a martial law regime illustrates this best. After a short experiment with elections and civilian control, Myanmar has returned to military rule but one in which contestation by the people has turned to civil war. While this may seem alien to Pakistanis, it is worrying that in parts of our country we, too, face a situation where the state appears to only control the cities. But what eventually determines the different state-society relationships in these countries? Why is Myanmar able to sustain military rule while Bangladesh is not? Or why has Pakistan, despite its close ties to the Middle East, not been able to impose a similar system of government? Now if I hadn’t learnt history in newsrooms and had read more, perhaps I could have answered some of these questions.
articles.author: Arifa Noor

articles.title: Cheer for conspiracy theories
articles.content: IT’S criminally easy and tempting to equate the idea of a conspiracy theory with gossip, unverified or motivated slander, usually pertaining to a high-profile political event, not excluding assassination. Call a story a conspiracy theory and kill an unanswered question with a smirk. Karl Popper was wary of pinning conspiracy theories onto individuals or institutions that could sway outcomes. He felt theories upfronting individuals or groups masked the trigger that prompted the event in the first place. I have my own conspiracy theory, if that is what one must call it, about the origins of the phrase and I pin it on the zealous and potent Zionist media. Technically, the phrase is ascribed to the 19th-century claim that Britain backed the Confederates in the American Civil War. But its first significantly notable use was the CIA’s attempt to debunk compelling questions about the assassination of JFK in 1963, particularly those leading to an Israeli hand. We’ll come to that. Nipping curiosity or agreeable narratives about the Israel lobby in the imperial hub of the US, which John Mearsheimer wrote a book about, remains a problem for Third World media consumers of Western-origin reports, which subtly or staunchly, knowingly or unwittingly root for the Zionist worldview. A new potentially important theory has surfaced about the over-chewed 9/11 narrative. Renowned anti-establishment American anchor Jimmy Dore interviewed Curt Weldon last week. The former 10-term Republican Congressman from Pennsylvania claimed new revelations into the affair. Weldon has spent decades claiming that a secret US military intelligence programme called Able Danger identified 9/11 hijackers before the attacks, and that the information was deliberately buried. Unsurprisingly, the claims routinely have been officially denied. Weldon served as Congressman from 1987 to 2007 and was vice chairman of the House Armed Services Committee. Before Congress, he was a lifelong volunteer firefighter, and he responded to the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing and the 9/11 attacks themselves. He has long argued that he lost his 2006 re-election bid as retaliation for his efforts to expose pre-9/11 intelligence failures. A new potentially important theory has surfaced about the over-chewed 9/11 narrative. Weldon’s new book, Able Danger: What the 9/11 Commission Never Told You, is scheduled for release today (Sept 22), and presents more than his hitherto detailed accounts of 9/11 allegations. The central claim is that a classified US Army data-mining programme called Able Danger used supercomputers to analyse intelligence databases and identified leading hijacker Mohamed Atta and his ‘Brooklyn cell’ over a year before 9/11. Weldon alleges that Able Danger team members tried to pass this information to the FBI at least three times by late 2000, but were blocked by military lawyers and bureaucratic ‘walls’. The 9/11 Commission released its report in 2004, and Able Danger’s findings were nowhere to be seen, the book laments. Weldon claims that the Commission deliberately omitted the most consequential facts to protect reputations and avoid accountability. He said his 2006 election loss was part of a “deep state” plot to prevent him from becoming Armed Services Committee chairman and exposing the truth. Why was Weldon bringing up the charges today, a quarter century after the event and what’s new? Dore believes the book offers a series of explosive allegations that go beyond the standard ‘Able Danger’ intelligence failure narrative, directly accusing senior US officials of not just failing to prevent 9/11, but of actively planning and covering it up. A personal memo Weldon retrieved from his archives ties the FBI raid on his daughter’s home three weeks before his 2006 election to the Able Danger cover-up. According to Weldon, the memo was sent by a top adviser to then defence secretary Donald Rumsfeld on the same day as the raid, and it stated: “Kurt, I warned you about Able Danger. Dick and Don are now going to destroy you.” He frames this as proof that his political destruction was orchestrated by Dick Cheney and Donald Rumsfeld to prevent him from becoming chairman of the House Armed Services Committee and exposing the programme. Weldon’s key assertions include the claim that the administration played games with Mohamed Atta’s identity, referring to him as ‘Mohamed Elsa’ to obscure that Able Danger had identified him. He also claims that army intelligence officer Erik Kleinsmith was ordered to destroy 2.5 terabytes of Able Danger data to prevent it from coming to light. Crucially, Weldon alleges that the US knew where Osama bin Laden was when it invaded Afghanistan and actually helped hide him in the Balochistan region (overlapping Iran and Pakistan), while sending American soldiers to die searching for him. He specifically accuses Commission director Philip Zelikow of leading a “whitewash”. It doesn’t matter much what Weldon is aiming to do with the new book. The point to note is that a former Congressman from the Republican circuit is making claims as an insider, which pits his version of the story against the familiar flat denial sans a winning logic. Comparing Kennedy’s assassination with 9/11 terrorism throws up several points to ponder, keeping Israel in the crosshairs. In the 9/11 event, five Israelis were arrested after being reported for allegedly dancing with joy, according to Chinese news reports of the attack. The arrests happened but the joy was apparently not proved and the men were freed. The FBI found no foreknowledge of the terror event with the men. In Kennedy’s case, a widely shared belief that the Mossad killed him is backed by a clear motive — Kennedy’s documented push for inspecting Israel’s illegal Dimona nuclear facility. Declassified files showed the CIA redacted ‘Israel’ among other countries. As many would prefer to see it, the bristling scorn Israel reserves for JFK’s legacy is readily reflected in Donald Trump’s furious plans to shut down the Kennedy Centre over false claims that it was a financial drain. Conspiracy theory? Dampen your enthusiasm till we come to the Epstein files, whenever they become public, if ever. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.
articles.author: Jawed Naqvi

articles.title: Autocratic legalism
articles.content: “THE power of a judicial branch, or of religious authorities who are the custodians of the law, lies only in the legitimacy that they can confer on rulers and in the popular support they receive as protectors of a broad social consensus. Gregory VII could force Henry [IV] to come to Canossa, but he could not actually depose him as emperor,” writes Francis Fukuyama in The Origins of Political Order. The judiciary has little coercive power to physically thwart excess by the executive. Nevertheless, even against an entrenched executive, there is one power which the judiciary retains. The power to deny the executive, which behaves in an ultra vires manner, the legitimacy it craves. This denial of legitimacy is nontrivial. Writing on the power of corporate groups to impose their will, Max Weber wrote in The Theory of Social and Economic Organisation that “Every such system attempts to establish and to cultivate the belief in its legitimacy”. North Korea, Equatorial Guinea, Russia, Belarus and Azerbaijan are headed by Kim Jong Un, Teodoro Mbasogo, Vladimir Putin, Alexander Lukashenko and Ilham Aliyev respectively, who are all dictators. Yet all these states hold elections and have legislative bodies and heads of government who exercise executive power in accordance with their respective constitution. Alas, hardly any of these states can be said to harbour true democracy. A recent paper published in the Journal of Democracy titled ‘How courts undermine democracy’ explains how courts grant to an excessive executive the legitimacy it craves, and perpetuate a cycle of ‘autocratic legalism’. The latter term refers to weaponisation of the law. Prof Kim Lane Scheppele in her essay Autocratic Legalism — published in the University of Chicago Law Review — argues that contemporary autocrats have mastered the use of legal and constitutional methods to weaken democratic institutions, consolidate power and do away with systems of checks and balances. The courts can deny the executive the legitimacy it wants. There is a ‘method to the madness’, and recognisable patterns, which enable the weaponisation of the law. Power is first captured through electoral or other means, and paves the way for filling the legislature with stalwarts or cronies. Once the legislature is controlled, it is employed to amend ordinary laws, as well as the constitution, so as to allow for what is called ‘courts capture’, ie, the courts are filled with compliant judges, and any judge who resists is sent home. Sometimes parallel or extraordinary courts, with jurisdiction over and above the existing ones, are established, to disturb and frustrate the legal hierarchy. With resulting ‘courts capture’, the system of ‘checks and balances’ is effectively dismantled. The heads of constitutional bodies and independent state agencies, which regulate elections, prosecute white collar crime, and survey and indict persons involved in anti-state activities, are replaced with ‘political commissars’. The state’s prosecutorial powers are unleashed on political opponents, and dissenting voices are silenced through legal processes. The ripples from this reorganisation of the state are so overwhelming that the bureaucracy either capitulates or is shuffled so as to sideline any officer who dares to raise his voice. The media is harnessed as an echo chamber, and thus, total control of the apparatuses of state is ensured. The doctrine of ‘autocratic legalism’ has the potential to turn judges into instruments of the executive. “Could any court having a discretion in the matter, issue an enforceable writ on the 8, 9 or 10 October against the government that had been brought into existence by the proclamation of president Iskander Mirza?” asked chief justice Munir in his subsequent writings ruminating on ‘The state vs Dosso’ (1958), and cited it as a reason for legitimising the first coup d’état in Pakistan. Justice Munir’s assessment of the enforceability of the writ, albeit accurate, was an utterly extra-legal consideration, and counterintuitive to his obligation to defend the constitution. The judicial acquiescence conferred legitimacy on a regime that was otherwise wanting. Resistance by the Supreme Court would not have reined in the usurpers; instead, it would have resulted in the whole court being sent home. Nevertheless, such an act would have denied to the usurpers the legitimacy they crave for, and demonstrated the highest form of judicial sacrifice — seldom extolled — which is pronouncing an unenforceable judgement, even at the peril of giving up one’s exalted office. Parallel or extraordinary courts, courts capture and amendments to the law and constitution to alter judicial hierarchy and electoral laws, concurrently, are ex-facie facets of ‘autocratic legalism’, and Pakistan ought to be circumspect.
articles.author: Asad-ul-Mulk

articles.title: Climate neutral
articles.content: SOUTH Asia has long viewed peace through the familiar language of power: territory, armies, missiles, borders, alliances and economic weight. China, India, Pakistan and Bangladesh sit at different points on this spectrum, and their relative capabilities are often measured in GDP, reserves, industrial capacity, defence budgets, troop strength, air power and nuclear weapons. Yet the recent climate- induced disaster in Nepal has introduced another measure of power, one that does not respect borders and cannot be deterred by military superiority. It is the capacity of a state to absorb shock, protect its people, maintain essential services and recover without falling into political or economic crisis. Seen through that lens, the region’s strategic map looks very different. China possesses an enormous economy, deep industrial capacity, extensive infrastructure and one of the world’s largest and most technologically advanced militaries. India combines a huge and rapidly growing economy with a large military, a nuclear arsenal, substantial manpower and an expanding industrial and technological base. Pakistan has considerable military capability, including nuclear weapons and a large standing force, but a smaller economy and tighter fiscal space. Bangladesh has a much smaller military and economic base, yet its experience with cyclones, floods, early-warning systems and community adaptation demonstrates that resilience is not simply a function of national wealth or firepower. The contrast is important. Military power is designed principally to impose costs on an adversary or prevent an adversary from doing so. Economic power provides resources to sustain that effort. Climate resilience performs a different function: it reduces the number of occasions on which societies are pushed into crisis in the first place. This matters because South Asia is unusually exposed to climate shocks. The monsoon is the region’s economic and ecological lifeline, while the Himalayas, great river systems, densely populated plains and low-lying coasts connect the fates of countries that frequently disagree on almost everything else. The World Bank estimates that more than half of South Asians have been affected by a natural disaster in the past two decades and climate change can turn economic strength into a temporary illusion. This distinction should reshape the meaning of security in South Asia. Climate stress can make confrontations more dangerous by weakening economies, intensifying competition over water and food, increasing displacement and narrowing governments’ room for manoeuvre. Defence must acquire another layer that protects from climate risks. The paradox is striking. States may spend billions acquiring weapons to prepare for threats that might never materialise while underinvesting in systems designed for disasters that are already occurring. Climate change is therefore like a progressively crippling disease. It does not ask whether a country is rich or poor, democratic or authoritarian, nuclear-armed or defenceless. It attacks the physical foundations on which every form of national power rests and undermines systems that support life. The lesson is not that armies are irrelevant. States still need credible defence, and deterrence remains essential in a region marked by unresolved disputes. The lesson is that defence must acquire another layer that protects from climate risks. The logic is compelling because climate risks cross borders. The most rational response is therefore neither surrender nor unilateralism, but mutually reinforcing mechanisms in which each country gains more from cooperation than from acting alone. The future balance of power in South Asia should consequently be measured in two columns. The first will continue to contain GDP, reserves, technology, troop numbers, missiles, aircraft and nuclear capability. The second should contain reservoirs, resilient cities, functioning hospitals, protected crops, reliable grids, emergency communications, early-warning coverage, fiscal buffers and the ability to recover quickly from catastrophe. The first column determines how much damage a state can threaten or withstand in war. The second determines whether its people can remain alive and its institutions functional when the enemy is a changing climate. That is the great neutralising force of climate change. The wisest strategy, therefore, is not to abandon power, but to broaden its definition. South Asia needs layers of defence that reinforce one another: military deterrence, economic resilience, environmental cooperation and human security. Peace will depend not only on preventing countries from fighting each other, but also on helping them survive the common shocks that none can defeat alone.
articles.author: Aisha Khan

articles.title: Civil service reform
articles.content: PAKISTAN cannot become a modern state as long as its bureaucracy continues to be organised around hierarchy, seniority and generalist recruitment. The system has become better at managing careers than solving problems. It rewards position rather than expertise and performance, and protects procedure more readily than outcomes. Moreover, a bureaucracy built primarily for routine administration can hardly meet the ever-growing economic, technological, environmental and social challenges confronting the government. It is against this backdrop that a ‘new’ civil servicerestructuring planhas been unveiled by the planning minister. The plan proposes professional cadres, seeks changes to the CSS examination, opens up senior posts to wider competition and links performance to rewards. It also proposes a new civil-service training structure. These ideas may not be new but they do make sense. However, the problem is that the plan represents a piecemeal approach. Several reform programmes were proposed in the last couple of decades; none was implemented due to resistance from bureaucracy and lack of political will. This plan could have provided a useful starting point for comprehensive civil service reform had it not cherry-picked proposals from an earlier reform exercise. The report, on which the new proposals draw, was prepared by the Institutional Reforms Committee headed by Dr Ishrat Husain in 2021, and covered recruitment, training, career progression, specialisation, performance management, accountability and the structure of the senior bureaucracy. It explicitly said that civil service reform had to be holistic. Reforming one segment of the system without addressing the others, it warned, could backfire. That raises the more important question: why are these proposals being put forward again, instead of building on the earlier blueprint? The government needs to explain what happened to the previous reform exercise, which of its recommendations were implemented, which were rejected and why. Instead, the government appears to have taken selected recommendations from it. That risks producing another reorganisation plan without actually changing the way the bureaucracy and state function. Civil service reform is not about creating new cadres, changing examination rules or merging training institutions. It is about changing incentives and institutional behaviour. The state needs specialists who can understand increasingly complex problems. It needs managers who can deliver. It needs promotion based on performance rather than seniority alone. And it needs accountability that applies to failure as much as success. Most importantly, reform requires consistency. The 2021 blueprint already provided much of the framework needed for this. If it fell short of anything, it should have been fixed instead of being discarded.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Restraint needed
articles.content: ISLAMABAD is bracing for two waves of protests. Not too long ago, for political parties to march towards the federal capital was nothing out of the ordinary. However, for some years now, Islamabad has increasingly come to be discussed in political circles as some kind of grand prize that is to be conquered or defended, depending on where one stands. In the days ahead, the Jamaat-i-Islami and the PTI are both expected to arrive at its gates, each with a very different list of demands in hand. The JI has set out to seek relief for the public from the harrowing prices of fuel these days, but there is no saying if that will be the limit of its ambition once the Margalla Hills are in sight. The PTI wants much more: it seeks to agitate for constitutional and democratic rights, elections and a fairer judiciary, as well as the release of, or at least some relief for, its jailed founder Imran Khan. Though both the JI and PTI sit on the opposition benches, it appears so far that their marches are taking place independently, and they would rather keep things that way. Given the rate at which containers are being laid out, trenches being dug and additional security requisitioned, it seems that the government is preparing not for a political event but an invasion. Even more concerning is the manner in which it has been arbitrarily arresting and detaining citizens, including Mr Khan’s sisters. This could turn an otherwise manageable political event into something much more confrontational. To avoid further escalation, the government must produce all detained leaders for judicial review and proceed by the book thereafter. Political protest is a right enshrined in the Constitution, and anyone, regardless of the party they belong to, is entitled to exercise that right as long as they do not take the law in their own hands. It would be commendable if, instead of a ‘thwart the protesters at all costs’ mentality, the government could designate protest sites before the caravans arrive so that it is not accused of subverting constitutional rights. In other words, the government would do well to avoid any unjustified use of force. The protesters, too, must stick to lawful means and avoid unnecessary confrontation. Both sides must remember that it is politics, not war, for which the protesters are marching to Islamabad.
articles.author: Editorial
